title: 2019 Year in Review
summary: The biggest event of 2019 was marrying my wife — she didn't cry at the wedding; I cried the whole way through
markdown:
2019 is over, so it's time to take stock of the year.

The biggest event of 2019 was marrying my wife. I still remember: she didn't cry at the ceremony. I cried from start to finish.

At work, I got a lot out of the projects:

- Pushed React Native as the core approach for our main product work
- Built a GitLab-based CI/CD pipeline for H5 (test and production) on Docker
- Set up Jenkins to produce App test builds
- Spun up internal Node services: batch app icon generation, batch payment QR codes, captcha lookup
- First year managing the frontend team

Where I fell short:

- Coding standards never really stuck in practice
- Not enough technical depth
- Management skills still thin
- Self-directed study plan — incomplete

2019 was an anxious year. I didn't know how to learn. Frameworks kept arriving; the landscape was noise. Should I double down on JavaScript fundamentals, or go deep on one framework? I spun on that for months. By year-end I'd settled: framework first — how it works, the patterns, the tricks — then peel back into the native JS underneath.

2019 was also the year I accepted that people want different things. Not everyone will proactively learn or polish every corner of a project. I will, though — find the problems, fix them.

It was the year I started understanding product work. Early on, every requirement change made me furious. Later I learned to listen, and to walk the product through iteration after iteration until it got better.

And watching senior folks ship blog after blog drove a simple point home: absolute follow-through and a real learning habit — that's how you get there.

Flags for 2020:

- I've always wanted a daughter. This year, that goal.
- One blog post a week, summarizing what I learned
- Dig deep into the React stack — from data flow, lifecycle, and components, through HOCs and Hooks, into whatever new land I find next
- Learn Swift, pick an open-source project, build a demo, prepare for cross-platform work
- At 170 jin, it's time to cut weight — start with 20 jin
